The **whale shark** (***Rhincodon typus***) is a slow-moving, [filter-feeding](Filter_feeder "Filter feeder") [carpet shark](Carpet_shark "Carpet shark") and the largest known [extant](Extant_taxon "Extant taxon") [fish](Fish "Fish") [species](Species "Species"). The largest confirmed individual had a length of 18.8 m (61.7 ft).[[8]](Whale_shark#cite_note-:1-8) The whale shark holds many records for size in the animal kingdom, most notably being by far the largest living nonmammalian [vertebrate](Vertebrate "Vertebrate"). It is the sole member of the genus ***Rhincodon*** and the only extant member of the family <Rhincodontidae>, which belongs to the subclass <Elasmobranchii> in the class <Chondrichthyes>. Before 1984 it was classified as *Rhiniodon* into Rhinodontidae.

The whale shark is found in open waters of the tropical oceans and is rarely found in water below 21 °C (70 °F).[[2]](Whale_shark#cite_note-iucn_status_19_November_2021-2) Studies looking at vertebral growth bands and the growth rates of free-swimming sharks have estimated whale shark lifespans at 80–130 years.[[9]](Whale_shark#cite_note-:4-9)[[10]](Whale_shark#cite_note-fishbase-10)[[11]](Whale_shark#cite_note-:5-11) Whale sharks have very large mouths and are filter feeders, which is a feeding mode that occurs in only two other sharks, the [megamouth shark](Megamouth_shark "Megamouth shark") and the [basking shark](Basking_shark "Basking shark"). They feed almost exclusively on [plankton](Zooplankton "Zooplankton") and small fishes and pose no threat to humans.

The species was distinguished in April 1828 after the harpooning of a 4.6 m (15 ft) specimen in [Table Bay](Table_Bay "Table Bay"), South Africa. [Andrew Smith](Andrew_Smith_(zoologist) "Andrew Smith (zoologist)"), a military doctor associated with British troops stationed in [Cape Town](Cape_Town "Cape Town"), described it the following year.[[12]](Whale_shark#cite_note-12) The name "whale shark" refers to the fish's size: it is as large as some species of whale.[[13]](Whale_shark#cite_note-13) In addition, its filter feeding habits are not unlike those of [baleen whales](Baleen_whale "Baleen whale").

## Description

Whale sharks possess a broad, flattened head with a large mouth and two small eyes located at the front corners.[[14]](Whale_shark#cite_note-:2-14)[[15]](Whale_shark#cite_note-:9-15) Unlike many other sharks, whale shark mouths are located at the front of the head rather than on the underside of the head.[[16]](Whale_shark#cite_note-16) A 12.1 m (39.7 ft) whale shark was reported to have a mouth 1.55 m (5.1 ft) across.[[17]](Whale_shark#cite_note-17) Whale shark mouths can contain over 300 rows of tiny teeth and 20 filter pads which it uses to [filter feed](Filter_feeder "Filter feeder").[[18]](Whale_shark#cite_note-FAO-18) The [spiracles](Spiracle_(vertebrates) "Spiracle (vertebrates)") are located just behind the eyes. The **great white shark** (***Carcharodon carcharias***), also known as the **white shark**, **white pointer**, or simply **great white**, is a species of large [mackerel shark](Lamniformes "Lamniformes") which can be found in the coastal surface waters of all the major oceans. It is the only known surviving [species](Species "Species") of its [genus](Genus "Genus") *<Carcharodon>*. The great white shark is notable for its size, with the largest preserved female specimen measuring 5.83 m (19.1 ft) in length and around 2,000 kg (4,410 lb) in weight at maturity.[[3]](Great_white_shark#cite_note-DMGO03-3) However, most are smaller; males measure 3.4 to 4.0 m (11 to 13 ft), and females measure 4.6 to 4.9 m (15 to 16 ft) on average.[[4]](Great_white_shark#cite_note-LGWS-4)[[5]](Great_white_shark#cite_note-Smithsonian-5) According to a 2014 study, the lifespan of great white sharks is estimated to be as long as 70 years or more, well above previous estimates,[[6]](Great_white_shark#cite_note-ADW-6) making it one of the longest lived [cartilaginous fishes](Chondrichthyes "Chondrichthyes") currently known.[[7]](Great_white_shark#cite_note-sciencedaily.com-7) According to the same study, male great white sharks take 26 years to reach sexual maturity, while the females take 33 years to be ready to produce offspring.[[8]](Great_white_shark#cite_note-livescience.com-8) Great white sharks can swim at speeds of 25 km/h (16 mph)[[9]](Great_white_shark#cite_note-9) for short bursts and to depths of 1,200 m (3,900 ft).[[10]](Great_white_shark#cite_note-deep-10)

The great white shark is arguably the world's largest-known extant macropredatory fish, and is one of the primary predators of [marine mammals](Marine_mammal "Marine mammal"), such as [pinnipeds](Pinniped "Pinniped") and [dolphins](Dolphin "Dolphin"). The great white shark is also known to prey upon a variety of other animals, including [fish](Fish "Fish"), other sharks, and [seabirds](Seabird "Seabird"). It has only one recorded natural predator, the [orca](Orca "Orca").[[11]](Great_white_shark#cite_note-11)

The species faces numerous ecological challenges which has resulted in international protection. The [International Union for Conservation of Nature](International_Union_for_Conservation_of_Nature "International Union for Conservation of Nature") lists the great white shark as a [vulnerable species](Vulnerable_species "Vulnerable species"),[[1]](Great_white_shark#cite_note-iucn_status_19_November_2021-1) and it is included in Appendix II of <CITES>.[[12]](Great_white_shark#cite_note-CITES-12) It is also protected by several national governments, such as <Australia> (as of 2018).[[13]](Great_white_shark#cite_note-au2013-13) Due to their need to travel long distances for seasonal migration and extremely demanding diet, it is not logistically feasible to

The **tiger shark** (***Galeocerdo cuvier***)[[2]](Tiger_shark#cite_note-ITIS-2) is a species of [ground shark](Ground_shark "Ground shark"), and the only extant member of the genus *<Galeocerdo>* and [family](Family_(Biology) "Family (Biology)") Galeocerdonidae. It is a large macropredator, with females capable of attaining a length of over 5 m (16 ft 5 in).[[3]](Tiger_shark#cite_note-FroesePauly-3) Populations are found in many [tropical](Tropical "Tropical") and [temperate](Temperate "Temperate") waters, especially around central <Pacific> islands. Its name derives from the dark stripes down its body, which resemble a [tiger](Tiger "Tiger")'s pattern, but fade as the shark matures.[[4]](Tiger_shark#cite_note-SharkInfo-4)

The tiger shark is a solitary, mostly nocturnal hunter. It is notable for having the widest food spectrum of all sharks, with a range of prey that includes [crustaceans](Crustacean "Crustacean"), [fish](Fish "Fish"), [seals](Pinniped "Pinniped"), [birds](Bird "Bird"), [squid](Squid "Squid"), [turtles](Turtle "Turtle"), [sea snakes](Hydrophiinae "Hydrophiinae"), [dolphins](Dolphin "Dolphin"), and even other, smaller sharks. It also has a reputation as a "garbage eater",[[4]](Tiger_shark#cite_note-SharkInfo-4) consuming a variety of inedible, man-made objects that linger in its stomach. Tiger sharks have only one recorded natural predator, the [orca](Orca "Orca").[[5]](Tiger_shark#cite_note-killerwhales-5) It is considered a [near threatened species](Endangered_species "Endangered species") because of [finning](Shark_finning "Shark finning") and fishing by humans.[[1]](Tiger_shark#cite_note-iucn_status_19_November_2021-1)

The tiger shark is second only to the [great white](Great_white_shark "Great white shark") in recorded fatal attacks on humans, but these events are still exceedingly rare.[[6]](Tiger_shark#cite_note-flmnh-6)[[7]](Tiger_shark#cite_note-7)

## Taxonomy

The shark was first described by [Peron](Fran%C3%A7ois_P%C3%A9ron "François Péron") and [Lesueur](Charles_Alexandre_Lesueur "Charles Alexandre Lesueur") in 1822, and was given the name *Squalus cuvier*.[[3]](Tiger_shark#cite_note-FroesePauly-3) [Müller](Johannes_Peter_M%C3%BCller "Johannes Peter Müller") and [Henle](Friedrich_Gustav_Jakob_Henle "Friedrich Gustav Jakob Henle") in 1837 renamed it *Galeocerdo tigrinus*.[[6]](Tiger_shark#cite_note-flmnh-6) The genus, *Galeocerdo*, is derived from the Greek *galeos*, which means shark, and *kerdo*, the word for fox.[[6]](Tiger_shark#cite_note-flmnh-6) It is often colloquially called the man-eater shark.[[6]](Tiger_shark#cite_note-flmnh-6)

content:
Based on the research, here are the **four largest fish** and what they eat:

## 1. **Whale Shark** (*Rhincodon typus*)
- **Maximum size:** 18.8 meters (61.7 ft), 21.5 tonnes
- **Diet:** Exclusively **plankton and small fishes**. It is a gentle filter feeder that uses 300 rows of tiny teeth and 20 filter pads to strain tiny organisms from the water. Unlike most sharks, its mouth is positioned at the front of its head rather than underneath.

## 2. **Basking Shark** (*Cetorhinus maximus*)
- **Maximum size:** 14 meters (46 ft), 5.2 tonnes
- **Diet:** **Plankton**. It's one of only three plankton-eating shark species in the world. The basking shark is a slow-moving filter feeder with greatly enlarged mouth and highly developed gill rakers that catch plankton as water flows through. It swims at the water's surface "basking" to feed.

## 3. **Great White Shark** (*Carcharodon carcharias*)
- **Maximum size:** 7 meters (23 ft), 3.3 tonnes
- **Diet:** **Marine mammals** (seals, sea lions, dolphins, other marine animals), along with various **fish species, other sharks, and seabirds**. It's the world's largest-known extant macropredatory fish and a primary predator of marine mammals.

## 4. **Tiger Shark** (*Galeocerdo cuvier*)
- **Maximum size:** 7.5 meters (25 ft), 3.1 tonnes
- **Diet:** Has the **widest food spectrum of all sharks**. Its prey includes **crustaceans, fish, seals, birds, squid, turtles, sea snakes, dolphins, and smaller sharks**. It's also known as a "garbage eater" due to consuming various inedible man-made objects found in the ocean.

**Interesting Note:** The two largest fish (whale shark and basking shark) are both gentle filter feeders that eat microscopic plankton, while the two next largest (great white and tiger sharks) are apex predators that hunt much larger prey.
